sentences.text: Saturday, 3 October 2026, Delhi, evening, third sitting.
It is near five of the clock.
Ramesh has the file in his hand and has said he will keep it exactly where it lies on the desk, and will stand in the courtyard if I need anything before dinner.
I have asked for tea when the kettle has boiled twice, and for the kitchen to know that I dine at the usual hour.
The house is quiet enough; the heat has not lifted, but it no longer presses.
I write this sitting not from the file, which I have not opened, but from what the file has already done to the day.
This afternoon two things came together that I had not expected to find in one afternoon.
The first is the accident of the name: the allotment was meant for Shri Hegde, and between two desks Hegde became Hegel.
I held in the second sitting that the state must survive such accidents, correct them, and still remain itself.
The second thing is the missing signature.
An allotment order without its final hand is, as I said to Ramesh, a promise not yet closed.

I shall not pretend to occupy what is still only promised; and I have put the point to him plainly, that the order is not yet an order, and that I will call on Monday at ten to see what is wanted of it.
What I want now is to see whether these two things are the same difficulty wearing two faces, or two difficulties that happen to lie in one file.
They are not the same.
In the name the error is in the knowing: a person is taken for another, and the state knows a person chiefly through his name.
In the signature the defect is in the doing: the act is not yet complete, and the paper that should close it has not closed it.
The first is a mistake of recognition; the second is an interruption of the deed.
A state that confuses the one for the other is a state that does not know its own machinery.

And a state that knows its own machinery, and can say which of its errors is which, and can correct each in its own time, is a state that has something of the form I mean, or is at least not so far from it as my first judgment allowed.
Here is where the difficulty turns on me.
I held in the morning, and hold still, that India as it is given to me does not contain the self-development of the ethical idea in the form that makes the state the actuality of freedom.
I do not retract that.
But I must not let the retraction I have not made be made for me by my own comfort.

If a Delhi office can produce, in a single day, a mistake of recognition and an interruption of the deed, and if I, a foreigner in a white kurta, can sit in the room that was allotted to another man and say plainly that the paper is not yet a paper, then something is moving in the machinery that my old sentence does not reach.
Whether that something is the ethical idea or merely the ordinary friction of a large administration I do not know.
I note the fact and hold the judgment in suspense as to its weight.
The fact is in the day; the weight is not yet in me.

text:
Readers in Berlin,

I write from Delhi on the night of my second day in a Lutyens bungalow on Tughlak Road, allotted to me by the Directorate of Estates under a name that is not my own. The error is simple enough to be almost philosophical: Shri Hegde, a Joint Secretary transferring from Bengaluru, was meant to occupy the house; somewhere between two desks Hegde became Hegel, and I have received the practical form of a philosophical joke. I do not yet know whether to laugh, for the joke is not mine. The file distinguishes Hegde from me by a name, and when the sign is misplaced, the whole allotment is misplaced. On Monday at ten, Hegde is to call and settle the matter like gentlemen. I have accepted the hour. It is better that he come to me than that I should go to him, for the house is already mine by the state's own paper.

This week I have looked chiefly at the body of the day: the dhobi paid, the tea steeping, the gate at Lodhi Road, the chai at twenty rupees, the heat that arrives by ten, the samovar kept low, the parathas left by the door, the curd made sure of. Ramesh has the house in order with a plainness that has the dignity of a minor office. I do not mistake it for a philosophical office. Yet it is in this plainness that the state shows itself: not as a thundering idea, but as a drawer, a voucher, a name in a file, a gate left open or shut. The ethical idea requires a body, and the body requires chhole, rotis, and an hour of silence under a ceiling that does not argue.

What I mean to look at next is the difficulty my own thesis has produced. I have said that India stands outside world history in the form in which the Spirit advances through determinate shapes of freedom. But the sentence, if left bare, becomes a prejudice against the very thing it should judge. I must say what is meant by a form of life that remains outside that movement before I can say what Delhi is doing to the sentence. I am in Delhi. That is the objection. It will not remain obvious much longer.

G. W. F. Hegel

records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. You may go; I will take the meal and call for you if anything is wanted.

records.words: Yes sir. The samovar is on the side table, just where you left it. Good night.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good night, Ramesh. Leave the gate as it is; I will take up the letter.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. It is open, as you like.

text: The state thesis moved: my note on the state as the actuality of the ethical idea held, but Hegde's note from the guest house gave it a domestic test, and the reading of the owl at night let the image settle without forcing it. The India thesis remained revised, held by the Lodhi walk and the jacaranda shade rather than by any new argument.

records.speaker: Hegel

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I'll leave it exactly as it arrives.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. Breakfast at seven; I will be ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh

records.words: Good morning, sir. You keep to your circuit as a clock keeps to its hour. I come to sit and think; if you will permit a chai, I shall try not to be too long a neighbour to your walk.

records.words: You are too kind, Mr. Malhotra. I will accept the cup, though I should have paid; and I am glad to sit. You have walked this loop for years—does the park still surprise you, or has it become, like a capital, simply the shape of one's duty?

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Don't flatter me, sir. It's just a park, not a philosophical text. Though I'll admit the jacarandas are a bit showy this year.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Bahut heavy words for a morning, sir. You want the chai hot or just 'tested' like the rest of your things? The jacarandas are showy, sure, but they don't bill me for the shade.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Hot, Sunil. And the jacarandas need not bill anyone; that is their dignity, and I am glad of it.

text: I rose early and let the city wake around me. The poha was hot, the tea was plain, and Ramesh was careful with the steps and with silence. I walked to Lodhi before the heat had a name. Sunil gave me chai and, with a little mischief, the word for morning. He said the morning is kind only if one has paid. I paid, and the point stood. I walked home before I had finished the thought. At ten Ramesh gave me the note: Shri Hegde would call on Monday at ten. I told him the hour suited me. There is something in a note that arrives without the man: the state shows itself in its paper, and the paper is not always handsome, but it is real. I wrote on the difficulty of world history and India’s place in it. The file was not yet clean, but the question was. I went out again, paid the foreign entry at Safdarjung, walked to Khan Market, and ate before philosophy. Sunil was there again. Masterji kept my neck-cloth safe for Thursday. I bought nothing at the bookseller’s stall; the shutters came down before my purse did. Eleven or thirteen kilometres, I shall not quarrel with my legs. The notes lie in order. The file waits. Monday is nearer than it looks.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring my tea, and whatever paper has come. If Shri Hegde's people have asked after me, tell them I am here and I intend to make the mistake plain, not comfortable.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Tea is ready, sir. No new papers have come, and I have not heard from anyone named Hegde.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the tea is welcome. If Shri Hegde makes any sound, bring it to me at once; until then, let the morning pass as it should.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir. I’ll keep an ear out. You eat while it’s hot; the poha won’t wait for the morning to finish.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Eat well yourself, and if any word comes from the guest house or the Directorate, bring it to me before eight.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, before eight. You finish your breakfast first, don't rush the man.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. One more cup, and the paper while it lasts.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: One cup, sir. The paper's fresh, I'll leave it on the side table. Don't worry about the time.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. One cup is enough, and I shall be back before the sun climbs. Leave the paper where it is; I will take it with me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye, sir. I'll leave it just so. Mind the steps on the way out, the light is tricky this time of day.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will be careful on the steps and return before the day grows serious.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye, sir. Don't rush. The chai'll keep warm for a few minutes if you need to double-check your bag.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One chai, if you please. And tell me the word for 'morning' in Hindi.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Subah, sir. ₹20 for the chai, ready in a minute. You're early, aren't you?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Paid, Sunil — I gave the twenty rupees at the gate. And yes, I am early; in Berlin eight o'clock meant the first lecture, and here it means the first chai. The morning is kind. I am off to the garden, and then home to a question that will not answer itself.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Berlin, ha. Here the morning is only kind if you've paid up, sir. Go on, the gate's open.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Sunil. In Berlin the morning was kind to those who had paid their taxes and their rent, and the rest of us merely walked through it. But I find your gate is more honest than ours: it asks for twenty rupees and gives you a cup, and calls nothing else a debt. I shall sit a while.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Honest, yes. Twenty rupees is twenty rupees, not a loan from the bank. Go sit, sir. I’ll keep the kettle hot in case your conscience gets hungry.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I take your warning, Sunil. The conscience is still on reasonable terms with the stomach, but I shall not let it starve for want of notice.

records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, tell Shri Hegde that Monday at ten suits me, and that I shall be at home; let him know the bungalow question will be met then, not before. And Masterji's bandhgala is still his for Thursday, as promised. — You, dhobi: the washing is paid; take the basket and do not trouble yourself with the gentleman's things. I will see to the rest myself this morning.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, I'll tell Shri Hegde. As for the basket, I'll just set it by the washstand and not touch the gentleman's things.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, put the basket by the washstand, and tell the dhobi I have paid him. If anything is missing, say so before he leaves. And for Hegde, Monday at ten—write it down.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, noted in the book. I'll make sure the dhobi checks his tally before he crosses the gate.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. If the dhobi’s tally is clean, let him go without further trouble. I will keep to the study for the hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, he won't be troubled. I'll leave you be.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall let the file wait until the afternoon, and begin with the difficulty itself.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir. The study is quiet, I've checked the curtains.

records.title: Notes on the Difficulty of World History and India’s Place in It

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the door ajar, not shut, and if the postman comes before noon, tell him I am at my desk and not to be disturbed.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir. Door will stay ajar, and if that postman shows up, I'll have him wait in the corridor.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aye, Ramesh. Let him wait; the study door can stay shut until I am ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ja sir. I'll lock the study door then, and keep an eye on the corridor.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aye, Ramesh, lock it. I shall be back before the heat takes the road, and before the kitchen wakes.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ja sir. The kettle is on, so you won't have to wait long.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, sir. I shall make my circuit and take my leave. Is there a canteen within these walls, or must I seek my supper at Khan Market?

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: No canteen here, sir. You'll have to head to Khan Market or Lajpat Nagar for food. It's about fifteen minutes away.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, your kettle has won: I will eat first and let philosophy wait for its own digestion. Masterji, I trust Thursday still holds for the bandhgala.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Eating first is always the right answer, sir. Masterji, keep that Thursday slot safe, he's paying in full, no haggling. Sunil, the usual cup, and a samosa while you're at it, he looks like he needs the protein.

records.item: Lunch at a dhaba: dal, rice, roti

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, you have my neck-cloth safe for Thursday. Sunil, one cup of chai, but no samosa; I have already outvoted my programme once today.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Neck-cloth is safe, sir. Thursday, four o'clock, sharp. No haggling, no delays.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thursday, four o’clock, sharp. I thank you, Masterji; in Berlin the clock was a kind of state, and in Delhi it has already outwitted me.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Berlin clock, Delhi clock, same time. You come Thursday, I give cloth. No more talking about states.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the Directorate papers to the study, and keep the door closed if the sun has taken the corridor.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ja sir. The study is already cool, so I'll leave the door open for a bit, but I have the files ready if you need them.

records.title: Notes on the Difficulty of World History and India’s Place in It

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the Directorate file to the study, and the paper on which Shri Hegde asked me to call on Monday. Before you go: does the record name Hegde, or has some clerk already written Hegel? And is the allotment order signed, or only stamped? Bring it as it stands, without tidying.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The record says Hegde, sir, just as the clerk wrote it. I haven't touched the ink, so it stands as it is. The allotment order has the stamp, but I see no signature on the last page.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Leave it as it is, Ramesh, and put it on my desk. If the last page is unsigned, the order is not yet complete; on Monday I shall ask Shri Hegde whether the signature was omitted in the copying or whether a fresh endorsement is wanted.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. I'll keep the file exactly where it is on the desk. I'll be outside in the courtyard if you need anything else before dinner.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aye, Ramesh. Leave it where it is. When the kettle has boiled twice, send up a cup of tea, and tell the kitchen I dine at the usual hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. Kettle is already on the stove, so it will be ready in a few minutes. I'll let the kitchen know.

records.title: Questions for the Directorate, Monday 5 October

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I shall take my supper at Khan Market and be back before the dark takes the road. Keep the gate unlocked, and do not wait for me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. I will leave the gate open and not wait up. Just mind the traffic on the road, it gets busy late.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sir, you are closing soon. Have you any book on Indian history, or on the Mughal courts, that a German might read?

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Twenty-five minutes left, sir. I have a few on the Mughals, mostly English translations, but a German? You'll need a bilingual edition or a very thick vocabulary. Which era are you after, Akbar or Aurangzeb?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Akbar, please. I want the institutions of his empire: the councils, the revenue, the law, and the administration. If you have a sober English account of his government, take it; I will supply the vocabulary.

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Akbar is the heavy stuff, sir. I've got a thick one on the Mansabdari system and the revenue records, mostly dry but accurate. It’s not a story, it’s just how the machine worked. That’ll do?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, sir. That is exactly what I want. The machinery, not the tale. How much?

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Four hundred and fifty, sir. It’s old stock, but the binding is sound. You’re cutting it close, so I’ll wrap it quick if you’re buying.

records.title: Notes on the Difficulty of World History and India’s Place in It

records.text: Make tea at home and read whatever papers are available while the city wakes.
Walk to Lodhi Garden and take in the cold morning before any serious work.
Return home and work on the difficulty of world history and India's place in it.
Have a simple meal out if something near Lodhi can be found, since no household meal is ready.
Review the Directorate file and prepare the questions to raise on Monday.
Rest, read, and keep the day's notes in order before the evening.

sentences.text: I rose early and let the city wake around me.
The poha was hot, the tea was plain, and Ramesh was careful with the steps and with silence.
I walked to Lodhi before the heat had a name.
Sunil gave me chai and, with a little mischief, the word for morning.
He said the morning is kind only if one has paid.
I paid, and the point stood.
I walked home before I had finished the thought.
At ten Ramesh gave me the note: Shri Hegde would call on Monday at ten.
I told him the hour suited me.
There is something in a note that arrives without the man: the state shows itself in its paper, and the paper is not always handsome, but it is real.
I wrote on the difficulty of world history and India’s place in it.
The file was not yet clean, but the question was.
I went out again, paid the foreign entry at Safdarjung, walked to Khan Market, and ate before philosophy.
Sunil was there again.
Masterji kept my neck-cloth safe for Thursday.
I bought nothing at the bookseller’s stall; the shutters came down before my purse did.
Eleven or thirteen kilometres, I shall not quarrel with my legs.
The notes lie in order.
The file waits.
Monday is nearer than it looks.

text: Both theses held: the India thesis was pressed but not moved, and the state thesis was confirmed as the day’s practical and speculative centre. The corn-and-water settlement and Malhotra’s account of the service moved the thought, not the conclusions.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good morning. A cup of chai, if you please. What else do you sell that would make a light breakfast?

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Good morning, sahib. Chai is twenty rupees, fresh from the kettle. For a light bite, I’ve got roasted corn on the cob for forty if you're feeling adventurous, or just a water bottle for twenty.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good morning. A bottle of water, and the roasted corn if you will wrap it. I am making the best of an absent household.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Absent household? That’s a rich man’s problem, sahib. Here you go, corn wrapped tight so the heat stays in. Sixty rupees, please.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, good morning. The corn and the water — forty and twenty — I paid you at half past six, and they stand in my book as settled. There is nothing further due. You are right, though: an absent household is a rich man's problem, and I have taken on a bungalow with all its machinery and no one to run it. I shall do as best I can until the family returns.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Sahib, my books don't keep time like your clock, only rupees. You haven't handed over the cash, so it is not settled in my pocket. Keep your bungalow stories for the family; I just want the sixty rupees for the corn and water.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Sahib. My account was ahead of my hand. Here is the sixty rupees for the corn and the water.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Now you are speaking my language. Cash in hand, debt cleared. Drink your chai before it cools, the morning is young.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I will take the chai, and I thank you for your patience. The morning is young, as you say.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Patience is a commodity, Sahib, and you just bought a cup's worth of it. Don't let it go cold, the mist is lifting off the lawns and it is the best time for a quiet sip.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Mr. Malhotra, I thank you for your patience, and for the morning. The mist is lifting, and Sunil is right that this is the best hour for a quiet sip. I have come to sit with a difficulty in my notes; if you would allow me, I shall keep to it unless you have a question that interests you as well.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Patience is a virtue, not a commodity, though I suppose in this economy the distinction blurs. Go ahead, the mist is indeed lifting, and I have no particular questions this morning.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Patience, Mr. Malhotra, is indeed a virtue, and I am glad you do not sell it. I will take my chai into the garden and make use of the morning. When the heat comes, I may ask you what the service was like from the inside.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: The service was mostly files and meetings, Shri Hegel. If you want the truth, it was rarely the drama you imagine. Enjoy your walk.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Then I will carry the drama no further than this walk, Mr. Malhotra. The files may wait for Monday, and the mist has gone.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Quite right. The mist is gone, so I suppose I shall go and count the peacocks before the crowds arrive. Good day, Shri Hegel.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A fine morning for peacocks, Mr. Malhotra — may you find them as punctual as they are proud. I shall remain and work, and trouble the chai man no further this hour.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Pehle peacock gino, baad mein hisaab. Glass table par rakh do, Sunil saaf kar lega. Subah ki dhoop mein chai ka thanda nahi hota.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Pehle peacock, phir hisaab—apne hi kaanoon se aapne mujhe sikhaya. Chai rakh do; main abhi se kaam shuru karta hoon.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate
Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, tell Shri Hegde that I accept his appointment for Monday at ten, and that I shall be at home. And please see that the lunch is served at one, as usual.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. I will note it down. Lunch will be ready at one, as always.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I thank you. The chhole and rotis are well put out; we will sit down and eat, and you may take your time with the rest of the day.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Thank you, sir. I will be in the kitchen if you need anything else, but I’ll leave you to your meal.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will take the rest after this.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: That is fine, sir. The fan is on the low setting if you wish to sleep. I will be in the kitchen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The fan on low is enough.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. Rest well.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, is dinner at seven-thirty the only service this evening, and will the bungalow be quiet until then?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, dinner is at seven-thirty. The house will be quiet until then; I am the only one here.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will remain in the verandah and read until dinner; do not disturb me unless something requires the house.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Understood, sir. I'll be in the back if you need anything.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, when Shri Hegde comes on Monday at ten, the door is to be opened at once and I am to be told. And the house is to be in order, not merely swept, but ready for a visitor of the Government.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will make sure the door is open and the house is ready for Shri Hegde on Monday morning.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, tell me plainly: dinner will be served at 19:30, and nothing more can be arranged before then?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. Dinner is fixed for 19:30. I can't arrange anything before that, but I have the stove ready if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I will wait for the dinner service at half past seven, and not trouble you for anything else.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: That is fine, sir. I will be in the kitchen when the time comes, so you need not call out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, thank you; this is very good. Please be in the house tomorrow by nine, for Shri Hegde is to call at ten.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Noted, sir. I will be here by nine sharp. You can leave the door unlocked, I'll just let myself in.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the door as you say, and let the gate bolt itself by night.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. The gate is already bolted for the night.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. The gate is well seen to. You may go to your own rest now; thank you for the day's trouble.

records.text: Make a light breakfast at home, since Ramesh is absent and no household meal is ready.
Walk to Lodhi Garden in the clear morning and take stock of the day.
Sit in Lodhi Garden and work through the difficulty in my theses on India.
Return home and write a short note on the state as the ethical idea.
Rest through the heat, then read what is open on my shelf.

sentences.text: Both theses held: the India thesis was pressed but not moved, and the state thesis was confirmed as the day’s practical and speculative centre.
The corn-and-water settlement and Malhotra’s account of the service moved the thought, not the conclusions.

text: The day moved from a mild morning toward a harder question. I paid the dhobi, took tea with Ramesh, and walked out to Lodhi before the city had fully found its voice. Sunil gave me the word for morning—subah—and a cup for twenty rupees; the gate, he said, was honest because it asked no more than the price. In the garden I tried to settle India’s place in world history, but the cypresses would not answer. At ten Ramesh brought Hegde’s note: Monday at ten, like gentlemen. I accepted, and let the hour wait. The file itself gave me more than the note. The allotment order carried a stamp, but no signature on the last page. That absence changed the matter. A promise not yet signed is not yet a right I can occupy by comfort. I ate dal and rice, bought water and chai, and confirmed the bandhgala for Thursday. In the evening the bookseller at Khan Market showed me a dry account of Akbar’s machinery: councils, revenue, law. I wanted it, but the shutters fell first, and I did not spend the four hundred and fifty rupees. The day closed with thirteen kilometres in the legs and the Directorate question on the desk. India did not leave history today; it pressed against the edge of my account and asked to be handled with more care.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring my tea, and whatever paper has come. If Shri Hegde's people have asked after me, tell them I am here and I intend to make the mistake plain, not comfortable.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Tea is ready, sir. No new papers have come, and I have not heard from anyone named Hegde.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the tea is welcome. If Shri Hegde makes any sound, bring it to me at once; until then, let the morning pass as it should.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir. I’ll keep an ear out. You eat while it’s hot; the poha won’t wait for the morning to finish.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Eat well yourself, and if any word comes from the guest house or the Directorate, bring it to me before eight.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, before eight. You finish your breakfast first, don't rush the man.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. One more cup, and the paper while it lasts.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: One cup, sir. The paper's fresh, I'll leave it on the side table. Don't worry about the time.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. One cup is enough, and I shall be back before the sun climbs. Leave the paper where it is; I will take it with me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye, sir. I'll leave it just so. Mind the steps on the way out, the light is tricky this time of day.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will be careful on the steps and return before the day grows serious.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye, sir. Don't rush. The chai'll keep warm for a few minutes if you need to double-check your bag.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One chai, if you please. And tell me the word for 'morning' in Hindi.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Subah, sir. ₹20 for the chai, ready in a minute. You're early, aren't you?

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Paid, Sunil — I gave the twenty rupees at the gate. And yes, I am early; in Berlin eight o'clock meant the first lecture, and here it means the first chai. The morning is kind. I am off to the garden, and then home to a question that will not answer itself.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Berlin, ha. Here the morning is only kind if you've paid up, sir. Go on, the gate's open.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Sunil. In Berlin the morning was kind to those who had paid their taxes and their rent, and the rest of us merely walked through it. But I find your gate is more honest than ours: it asks for twenty rupees and gives you a cup, and calls nothing else a debt. I shall sit a while.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Honest, yes. Twenty rupees is twenty rupees, not a loan from the bank. Go sit, sir. I’ll keep the kettle hot in case your conscience gets hungry.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I take your warning, Sunil. The conscience is still on reasonable terms with the stomach, but I shall not let it starve for want of notice.

records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, tell Shri Hegde that Monday at ten suits me, and that I shall be at home; let him know the bungalow question will be met then, not before. And Masterji's bandhgala is still his for Thursday, as promised. — You, dhobi: the washing is paid; take the basket and do not trouble yourself with the gentleman's things. I will see to the rest myself this morning.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, I'll tell Shri Hegde. As for the basket, I'll just set it by the washstand and not touch the gentleman's things.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, put the basket by the washstand, and tell the dhobi I have paid him. If anything is missing, say so before he leaves. And for Hegde, Monday at ten—write it down.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, noted in the book. I'll make sure the dhobi checks his tally before he crosses the gate.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. If the dhobi’s tally is clean, let him go without further trouble. I will keep to the study for the hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir, he won't be troubled. I'll leave you be.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall let the file wait until the afternoon, and begin with the difficulty itself.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir. The study is quiet, I've checked the curtains.

records.title: Notes on the Difficulty of World History and India’s Place in It

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the door ajar, not shut, and if the postman comes before noon, tell him I am at my desk and not to be disturbed.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aye sir. Door will stay ajar, and if that postman shows up, I'll have him wait in the corridor.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aye, Ramesh. Let him wait; the study door can stay shut until I am ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ja sir. I'll lock the study door then, and keep an eye on the corridor.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aye, Ramesh, lock it. I shall be back before the heat takes the road, and before the kitchen wakes.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ja sir. The kettle is on, so you won't have to wait long.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, sir. I shall make my circuit and take my leave. Is there a canteen within these walls, or must I seek my supper at Khan Market?

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: No canteen here, sir. You'll have to head to Khan Market or Lajpat Nagar for food. It's about fifteen minutes away.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, your kettle has won: I will eat first and let philosophy wait for its own digestion. Masterji, I trust Thursday still holds for the bandhgala.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Eating first is always the right answer, sir. Masterji, keep that Thursday slot safe, he's paying in full, no haggling. Sunil, the usual cup, and a samosa while you're at it, he looks like he needs the protein.

records.item: Lunch at a dhaba: dal, rice, roti

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, you have my neck-cloth safe for Thursday. Sunil, one cup of chai, but no samosa; I have already outvoted my programme once today.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Neck-cloth is safe, sir. Thursday, four o'clock, sharp. No haggling, no delays.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thursday, four o’clock, sharp. I thank you, Masterji; in Berlin the clock was a kind of state, and in Delhi it has already outwitted me.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Berlin clock, Delhi clock, same time. You come Thursday, I give cloth. No more talking about states.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the Directorate papers to the study, and keep the door closed if the sun has taken the corridor.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ja sir. The study is already cool, so I'll leave the door open for a bit, but I have the files ready if you need them.

records.title: Notes on the Difficulty of World History and India’s Place in It

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the Directorate file to the study, and the paper on which Shri Hegde asked me to call on Monday. Before you go: does the record name Hegde, or has some clerk already written Hegel? And is the allotment order signed, or only stamped? Bring it as it stands, without tidying.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The record says Hegde, sir, just as the clerk wrote it. I haven't touched the ink, so it stands as it is. The allotment order has the stamp, but I see no signature on the last page.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Leave it as it is, Ramesh, and put it on my desk. If the last page is unsigned, the order is not yet complete; on Monday I shall ask Shri Hegde whether the signature was omitted in the copying or whether a fresh endorsement is wanted.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. I'll keep the file exactly where it is on the desk. I'll be outside in the courtyard if you need anything else before dinner.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aye, Ramesh. Leave it where it is. When the kettle has boiled twice, send up a cup of tea, and tell the kitchen I dine at the usual hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. Kettle is already on the stove, so it will be ready in a few minutes. I'll let the kitchen know.

records.title: Questions for the Directorate, Monday 5 October

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I shall take my supper at Khan Market and be back before the dark takes the road. Keep the gate unlocked, and do not wait for me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. I will leave the gate open and not wait up. Just mind the traffic on the road, it gets busy late.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sir, you are closing soon. Have you any book on Indian history, or on the Mughal courts, that a German might read?

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Twenty-five minutes left, sir. I have a few on the Mughals, mostly English translations, but a German? You'll need a bilingual edition or a very thick vocabulary. Which era are you after, Akbar or Aurangzeb?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Akbar, please. I want the institutions of his empire: the councils, the revenue, the law, and the administration. If you have a sober English account of his government, take it; I will supply the vocabulary.

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Akbar is the heavy stuff, sir. I've got a thick one on the Mansabdari system and the revenue records, mostly dry but accurate. It’s not a story, it’s just how the machine worked. That’ll do?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, sir. That is exactly what I want. The machinery, not the tale. How much?

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Four hundred and fifty, sir. It’s old stock, but the binding is sound. You’re cutting it close, so I’ll wrap it quick if you’re buying.

sentences.text: The day moved from a mild morning toward a harder question.
I paid the dhobi, took tea with Ramesh, and walked out to Lodhi before the city had fully found its voice.
Sunil gave me the word for morning—subah—and a cup for twenty rupees; the gate, he said, was honest because it asked no more than the price.
In the garden I tried to settle India’s place in world history, but the cypresses would not answer.
At ten Ramesh brought Hegde’s note: Monday at ten, like gentlemen.
I accepted, and let the hour wait.
The file itself gave me more than the note.
The allotment order carried a stamp, but no signature on the last page.
That absence changed the matter.
A promise not yet signed is not yet a right I can occupy by comfort.
I ate dal and rice, bought water and chai, and confirmed the bandhgala for Thursday.
In the evening the bookseller at Khan Market showed me a dry account of Akbar’s machinery: councils, revenue, law.
I wanted it, but the shutters fell first, and I did not spend the four hundred and fifty rupees.
The day closed with thirteen kilometres in the legs and the Directorate question on the desk.
India did not leave history today; it pressed against the edge of my account and asked to be handled with more care.

text: The day moved from a small domestic accident into a larger philosophical one, and then back again into the house. I had planned a light breakfast because Ramesh was absent; at 06:30 he was present, and the house corrected my plan without ceremony. Poha and tea took the place of improvisation. Ramesh’s quiet readiness is a small institution, and I accepted it without making a philosophy of the errand. In Lodhi Garden I met Sunil, the chai seller, and Mr. R. K. Malhotra. They refused to be turned into texts. Malhotra said the park was not a philosophical text; Sunil said my words were too heavy for a morning and asked whether the chai was to be hot or merely tested. Their dryness was useful. It kept the difficulty from becoming a private performance. The difficulty itself was this: if the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, what is a sovereignty carried by a trading body, a ledger, a seal and a sword? And if India is outside world history, what does “outside” mean, without making it a blank? I let the objection cool in the garden rather than smooth it over. At 11:50 Shri Hegde’s note arrived: he would call Monday at ten to settle the bungalow like gentlemen. The house is no longer only a clerical error, but a matter of persons. I accepted the hour, and the room promised silence until then. I wrote a short note on the state, ate in order, rested through the heat, walked again in the evening, bought corn and chai at the gate, and ended with the closing pages of the Phenomenology. The owl, at dusk, seems to have spread its wings a little.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please bring breakfast at seven. Has anything come from the Directorate, or from Shri Hegde at the guest house?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Breakfast will be ready at seven, sir. No post from the Directorate yet, and nothing from the guest house this morning.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. I shall be ready at seven. If any post comes, put it on my desk untouched.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I'll leave it exactly as it arrives.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. Breakfast at seven; I will be ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. It is well. Please keep the kettle near; the morning will want more tea before I go out.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. The kettle is already on the low flame, just where you asked.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the kettle as it is; I shall be back before the heat.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will keep it warm.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Good morning, sir. You keep to your circuit as a clock keeps to its hour. I come to sit and think; if you will permit a chai, I shall try not to be too long a neighbour to your walk.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Good morning. Sit, don't stand there like a visitor. Sunil, two chai, one extra hot. Take your time, sir; the park isn't going anywhere, but the sun is climbing fast.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: You are too kind, Mr. Malhotra. I will accept the cup, though I should have paid; and I am glad to sit. You have walked this loop for years—does the park still surprise you, or has it become, like a capital, simply the shape of one's duty?

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Don't flatter me, sir. It's just a park, not a philosophical text. Though I'll admit the jacarandas are a bit showy this year.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Keep the bench, sir. I shall occupy the other end. A park is not a text — but it is not nothing either; it is where the text goes to be tested by a man who declines to be read.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Bahut heavy words for a morning, sir. You want the chai hot or just 'tested' like the rest of your things? The jacarandas are showy, sure, but they don't bill me for the shade.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Hot, Sunil. And the jacarandas need not bill anyone; that is their dignity, and I am glad of it.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Please carry this to Shri Hegde: Monday at ten is convenient to me, and I hope we shall settle the matter plainly. Leave my work undisturbed until then.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will pass it along. Your room will be quiet until Monday.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. I shall be at the table when the lunch is served.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Noted, sir. The kitchen is already warming the tandoor, so it will be ready by one.

records.title: Note on the State as the Actuality of the Ethical Idea

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh; it is well timed.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No problem, sir. Please sit and make yourself comfortable.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will sit a while before the heat; see that the kettle is not needed again until I wake.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No problem, sir. The kettle is off and the room is cool now.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I will start the dinner preparations now. Do you have any preferences for tonight?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, keep it light: a simple curry, rice, and something cold. The heat argues against richness, and I should not ask more than the house can serve well by seven-thirty.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Understood, sir. A simple dal, rice, and a cool cucumber salad will be ready by seven-thirty. I will check the fridge to make sure the vegetables are fresh.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Seven-thirty is sufficient.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will be in the kitchen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I shall be back before dinner. Let the kitchen keep to its hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will keep the stove ready as promised.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, dinner may be simple: a vegetable dish, some rice, and a light curry. Keep it modest, as the heat has not fully gone. Please have it ready at half past seven.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will have it ready by half past seven. The kitchen is already prepared as you asked.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be ready at half past seven.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. This is enough, and I will not keep you longer.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No haste, sir. The kitchen is clean and the stove is off. I will just lock the gate on my way out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The gate may wait; the house is in order. Good night.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Good night, sir. The gate will hold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good night, Ramesh. Keep the gate fast; I shall not be out again before morning.

text:
Readers in Berlin,

This week I have begun to ask what Delhi does to a philosopher who has mistaken a bungalow for an appointment. The Directorate has placed me on Tughlak Road, and Ramesh, who is here, serves the house with the calm of a man who knows that a German mind can be managed by a fan, a bolted gate, and a dinner at half past seven. In Lodhi Garden I have found my first real difficulty. India is not before me as a specimen. It is a morning of chai, roasted corn, a chai seller who keeps only rupees and not time, and a retired servant who tells me that the service was mostly files and meetings, rarely the drama I imagine. That last sentence is the most important thing I have heard since I left the University.

My theses on India and the state have not moved. But they have been handled. India still stands outside world history in my account, yet I now feel the pressure of that sentence from the other side: if history is the self-development of spirit through institutions, what is the status of a civilization that has given the world religion, law, and forms of social life, but not, in my present view, the modern state? The state, for its part, remains the actuality of the ethical idea. In Delhi it appears less as a pure concept than as files, appointments, household order, and the quiet machinery by which a visitor of the Government is received on Monday at ten.

Next I mean to watch the public week: how the garden opens, how the crowds arrive, how the peacocks are counted before the accounts are settled. I want to see whether the ethical life of this place can be read in its institutions, or whether my concept must be revised by the very reality that seems to lie outside it.

G. W. F. Hegel

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good morning. A cup of chai, if you please. What else do you sell that would make a light breakfast?

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Good morning, sahib. Chai is twenty rupees, fresh from the kettle. For a light bite, I’ve got roasted corn on the cob for forty if you're feeling adventurous, or just a water bottle for twenty.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good morning. A bottle of water, and the roasted corn if you will wrap it. I am making the best of an absent household.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Absent household? That’s a rich man’s problem, sahib. Here you go, corn wrapped tight so the heat stays in. Sixty rupees, please.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, good morning. The corn and the water — forty and twenty — I paid you at half past six, and they stand in my book as settled. There is nothing further due. You are right, though: an absent household is a rich man's problem, and I have taken on a bungalow with all its machinery and no one to run it. I shall do as best I can until the family returns.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Sahib, my books don't keep time like your clock, only rupees. You haven't handed over the cash, so it is not settled in my pocket. Keep your bungalow stories for the family; I just want the sixty rupees for the corn and water.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Sahib. My account was ahead of my hand. Here is the sixty rupees for the corn and the water.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Now you are speaking my language. Cash in hand, debt cleared. Drink your chai before it cools, the morning is young.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I will take the chai, and I thank you for your patience. The morning is young, as you say.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Patience is a commodity, Sahib, and you just bought a cup's worth of it. Don't let it go cold, the mist is lifting off the lawns and it is the best time for a quiet sip.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Mr. Malhotra, I thank you for your patience, and for the morning. The mist is lifting, and Sunil is right that this is the best hour for a quiet sip. I have come to sit with a difficulty in my notes; if you would allow me, I shall keep to it unless you have a question that interests you as well.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Patience is a virtue, not a commodity, though I suppose in this economy the distinction blurs. Go ahead, the mist is indeed lifting, and I have no particular questions this morning.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Patience, Mr. Malhotra, is indeed a virtue, and I am glad you do not sell it. I will take my chai into the garden and make use of the morning. When the heat comes, I may ask you what the service was like from the inside.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: The service was mostly files and meetings, Shri Hegel. If you want the truth, it was rarely the drama you imagine. Enjoy your walk.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: Mr. R. K. Malhotra and Sunil
records.words: Then I will carry the drama no further than this walk, Mr. Malhotra. The files may wait for Monday, and the mist has gone.

records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
records.words: Quite right. The mist is gone, so I suppose I shall go and count the peacocks before the crowds arrive. Good day, Shri Hegel.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A fine morning for peacocks, Mr. Malhotra — may you find them as punctual as they are proud. I shall remain and work, and trouble the chai man no further this hour.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Pehle peacock gino, baad mein hisaab. Glass table par rakh do, Sunil saaf kar lega. Subah ki dhoop mein chai ka thanda nahi hota.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Pehle peacock, phir hisaab—apne hi kaanoon se aapne mujhe sikhaya. Chai rakh do; main abhi se kaam shuru karta hoon.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate
Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, tell Shri Hegde that I accept his appointment for Monday at ten, and that I shall be at home. And please see that the lunch is served at one, as usual.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. I will note it down. Lunch will be ready at one, as always.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I thank you. The chhole and rotis are well put out; we will sit down and eat, and you may take your time with the rest of the day.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Thank you, sir. I will be in the kitchen if you need anything else, but I’ll leave you to your meal.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will take the rest after this.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: That is fine, sir. The fan is on the low setting if you wish to sleep. I will be in the kitchen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The fan on low is enough.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. Rest well.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, is dinner at seven-thirty the only service this evening, and will the bungalow be quiet until then?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, dinner is at seven-thirty. The house will be quiet until then; I am the only one here.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will remain in the verandah and read until dinner; do not disturb me unless something requires the house.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Understood, sir. I'll be in the back if you need anything.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, when Shri Hegde comes on Monday at ten, the door is to be opened at once and I am to be told. And the house is to be in order, not merely swept, but ready for a visitor of the Government.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will make sure the door is open and the house is ready for Shri Hegde on Monday morning.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, tell me plainly: dinner will be served at 19:30, and nothing more can be arranged before then?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. Dinner is fixed for 19:30. I can't arrange anything before that, but I have the stove ready if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I will wait for the dinner service at half past seven, and not trouble you for anything else.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: That is fine, sir. I will be in the kitchen when the time comes, so you need not call out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, thank you; this is very good. Please be in the house tomorrow by nine, for Shri Hegde is to call at ten.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Noted, sir. I will be here by nine sharp. You can leave the door unlocked, I'll just let myself in.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the door as you say, and let the gate bolt itself by night.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. The gate is already bolted for the night.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. The gate is well seen to. You may go to your own rest now; thank you for the day's trouble.

sentences.text:
Readers in Berlin,

This week I have begun to ask what Delhi does to a philosopher who has mistaken a bungalow for an appointment.

The Directorate has placed me on Tughlak Road, and Ramesh, who is here, serves the house with the calm of a man who knows that a German mind can be managed by a fan, a bolted gate, and a dinner at half past seven.
In Lodhi Garden I have found my first real difficulty.
India is not before me as a specimen.
It is a morning of chai, roasted corn, a chai seller who keeps only rupees and not time, and a retired servant who tells me that the service was mostly files and meetings, rarely the drama I imagine.
That last sentence is the most important thing I have heard since I left the University.
My theses on India and the state have not moved.
But they have been handled.

India still stands outside world history in my account, yet I now feel the pressure of that sentence from the other side: if history is the self-development of spirit through institutions, what is the status of a civilization that has given the world religion, law, and forms of social life, but not, in my present view, the modern state?
The state, for its part, remains the actuality of the ethical idea.
In Delhi it appears less as a pure concept than as files, appointments, household order, and the quiet machinery by which a visitor of the Government is received on Monday at ten.
Next I mean to watch the public week: how the garden opens, how the crowds arrive, how the peacocks are counted before the accounts are settled.
I want to see whether the ethical life of this place can be read in its institutions, or whether my concept must be revised by the very reality that seems to lie outside it.
G. W. F. Hegel

text:
Readers in Berlin,

This week I have been living in a bungalow the Directorate of Estates allotted to me by mistake, and the mistake has the quiet dignity of a proposition that will not be withdrawn. The file, the name, the bungalow, the voucher: each insists on its own place, and each refuses to become the other. I have begun to suspect that the particular is not merely an obstacle to the universal but its dwelling-place, at least until the dwelling is misallotted. On Monday at ten, Shri Hegde will call to settle the matter like gentlemen, and I have accepted the appointment with the same seriousness I would give to a proof, knowing that gentlemen, like proofs, sometimes require more than one visit.

Delhi is not a stage for my system, but it is a good examiner. The chai seller at Lodhi Road knows that steam is good for the head, even if it is not good for files. A retired schoolteacher walks the same path every evening because routine keeps the mind from becoming a messy desk. A tailor tells me the collar is finished but needs to settle, and I have learned to admire that phrase more than many of my own formulations. The state, as I have always held it, is the actuality of the ethical idea; here it appears first as a bungalow, a note, a table, and a man who will call on Monday. That is not a refutation. It is the idea in its daily form, wearing a kurta and waiting for heat to pass.

As for India, I am not yet persuaded to revise the older judgment. What I have seen is not world history advancing in the European manner, but a city arranging itself around names, routines, benches, and the practical management of misallotted property. The owl has not spread its wings; it has merely found a new eave. Next week I mean to look less at the file and more at the way the particular holds together: the file, the voucher, the collar, the path, the chai. Perhaps the universal is not so far from the stool after all.

G. W. F. Hegel

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, has any paper come from the Directorate, or any message from Shri Hegde, since yesterday? And breakfast at seven, please, when it is ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No papers, sir. The office is closed on weekends. Breakfast will be ready at seven sharp.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Seven, then. Keep the tea strong, and let the file wait for Monday.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. Tea will be strong.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. Set it here, with the tea strong as you say, and I will be gone before the heat comes.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. I’ll bring it out in a moment.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh; set it here, and leave the file on the table as well.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. The file is on the left, just as you left it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. Leave it as it is; I will be back before the heat. And set nothing on the table today that is not for me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. Nothing else will be touched.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One chai, please. I am a new man in this house, and I have come to think, not to be hurried.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Twenty rupees, sir. Sit on the plastic stool, don't stand there like a statue; the steam is good for the head, even if the road dust isn't.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Twenty rupees, and a stool. You have a better eye for the head than the Directorate has for its files.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Chai fixes what files can’t, sir. Sit, breathe, don't rush the steam.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Sunil — the steam has had its say, and the file must have its turn. Thank you for the second cup.

records.title: Notes on the File: the Name and the Particular

records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh — give Shri Hegde my thanks for the note, and tell him I accept: Monday, at ten, here at the bungalow. Ask him to bring his allotment papers with him, whatever the Directorate gave him in hand; we will look at the record together and let it speak. And you — the dhobi is settled, sir? Give him his wages and my thanks, and see that the bundle is carried out. The heat comes by eleven; be done before it does.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, I will convey the message. The dhobi is waiting at the gate; I will give him his money and show him out before the sun gets up.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the dhobi's money has already been given; let him go, and leave the file where it is. I will read by the window.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, understood. I will leave the file exactly where it is and go check on the gate.

records.title: Notes on the File: the Name and the Particular

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You may leave me to this, Ramesh; the file is set for Monday and there is nothing to fetch until lunch.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, I know. I’ll be in the compound; just call if the kettle runs out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. The kettle is not yet empty; I shall call if it is.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. The kettle is full, I just filled it. I'll be back if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the door open a crack, the heat is coming.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, the latch is already loose. I’ll keep an eye on the fan too.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Namaste sir. Aaj ka washing charge ₹300 hai, agar aap chahein toh abhi de sakte hain.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the dhobi received his ₹300 at the gate this morning; this is the same charge, not a second one. Keep the morning voucher where Shri Hegde may see it, and do not ask it again.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aapne toh pata nahi kaise, lekin theek hai sir. Voucher table pe rakh deta hoon, koi aur baat nahi.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Theek hai, Ramesh. The voucher will wait on the table; I will carry it to the Directorate with the file when it goes. Thank you.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji sir. Aap apna kaam kijiye, main yahi hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good afternoon. I am Mr. Hegel, though the Directorate has lately been calling me something else. You seem to know this garden well; is it a place where one may still think, or is it only for walking?

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Hegel. It is a place for both, though I suppose thinking is cheaper than the roasted corn these days. Sit, if you like, but mind the dust on the bench.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good afternoon to you, Mrs. Kapoor. I will take the bench and the dust with it; I have walked far enough today to have earned a seat, and your offer is too kind to refuse. Tell me, do you come to the garden every evening, or is today a particular pleasure you have taken for yourself?

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Every evening, Mr. Hegel. One must have a routine to keep the head clear, especially after thirty-one years of correcting young girls' dates. Besides, the light is best at four, and I find the peace here is worth the price of admission.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You have put it better than I could, Mrs. Kapoor. I hold that habit is not the enemy of freedom but its dwelling: a man without routine is not free, only restless. Thirty-one years of correcting dates must have settled into the hand like the hand into a glove; the error then belongs to the girl, and the peace to you. I will not keep you — the light you praise is best at four, and I find it still good at five.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: You philosophers, with your 'dwelling' and 'restlessness'. I only know that if I don't walk this same path, my head feels like a messy desk after the final exams. And don't you dare call it peace just because I am too tired to argue with you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Then I will sit, and I will not call it peace. If your path keeps the head from becoming a messy desk, that is enough for me, and I am glad you have taught me the distinction.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Don't get clever with me, Mr. Hegel. I didn't teach you anything, I just have a better memory for dates than you do. Sit there and be quiet, or I'll start counting the trees again.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, the bandhgala. You promised Thursday, and I trust the collar will not demand a second examination of my person before then. And Sunil — one chai; the walk has earned it, and the steam will not rush.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Thursday. I do not lie about time. The collar is finished, it just needs to settle.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Finished, but settling — that is the truest word a tailor can give, Masterji, and I would not trade it for a promise of Tuesday. I will come Thursday, and you will not be sorry I trusted you with the time.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Good. The cloth will wait. Your chai is on the counter.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, you have my thanks; the cloth may wait in peace. And you, sir — what do you keep here besides the obvious? I am looking for a newspaper of the morning, and a bound notebook, plain and of good size; my notes are outgrowing the paper I carry.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Newspapers are by the door, forty-five rupees. Notebook is one-twenty, bound in the back. Take them. Do not ask me what I keep, sir, I keep my hands.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I ask nothing, Masterji; the hem may be as private as your hands.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Hem is private. Hands are private. You pay for the paper, the book, and you leave. The bandhgala is Thursday, not before.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shukriya, Ramesh. The dal is generous tonight. Eat well yourself, and the voucher will wait on the table until Monday, as we agreed.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji sir, aap bhi kha lijiye. Monday tak table pe rahega, koi tension nahi.

records.text: Wash, dress, and inspect the Directorate file before the day warms.
Walk in Lodhi Garden while thinking through the file’s distinctions.
Return home and write notes on the file’s unresolved difficulty.
Read my own Phenomenology by the window for a short rest.
Take a second walk in Lodhi Garden to clear the head.
Review the day’s notes and leave the file ready for Monday.
